e.etymology: An English surname for a man who was free-born and not a serf; in the United States it was also taken as a surname by people freed from slavery. It was a common first name in the 1800s.
The Spanish form of Late Latin Firminus, from firmus, firm or steadfast. Saint Fermin is the patron of Pamplona, honored each July at the festival with the running of the bulls.
A short form of Richard, from Germanic elements meaning ruler and strong, hardy.
e.note: Also the everyday word for wealthy.

e.etymology: A less common spelling of Leroy, from Old French le roy, the king, a surname that became an American first name in the 1800s.

assoc.t: Leeroy Jenkins, World of Warcraft battle-cry meme

e.etymology: From Greek Isidoros, Isis plus doron, gift. Despite the pagan goddess it was borne by early Christian saints, notably Isidore of Seville, and was later popular in Jewish families.
namesakes: Saint Isidore of Seville (7th-century scholar and bishop)

e.etymology: In the US mostly a spelling of Kaylee or Kylie. Kaili is also a separate Estonian name, a modern blend of Kai (Catherine) and Lii (Elizabeth).
The Greek word Christos, anointed one, the title of Jesus. In Greece it is an everyday given name, often merged with the like-sounding Chrestos, good or kind.
The surname of the Austrian composer Joseph Haydn, taken up as a first name in his honor, especially in Wales. In the US it is also used as a spelling of Hayden.
e.note: The composer's name is said HY-dun, but most people read the given name as HAY-dun.

e.etymology: A compound of Mary and Kate, the short form of Katherine. Its peak around 2001 followed the fame of actress Mary-Kate Olsen.
A K spelling of Carlos, the Spanish and Portuguese form of Charles, from Germanic karl, free man. Karlos is also the regular Basque spelling.
The English word, from Old English freodom. As a given name it belongs with Liberty and Justice, and its use peaked in the mid-1970s.
The Italian feminine form of Matteo, the Italian Matthew, from Hebrew Mattityahu, gift of the Lord.
A Spanish short form of Rigoberto, a Germanic name made of ric, ruler or power, and berht, bright.
An English surname meaning son of Reynold, the Norman form of a Germanic name built from ragin, counsel, and wald, rule.

assoc.t: actors Ryan Reynolds and Burt Reynolds (surname)

e.etymology: The Italian form of Gisela and Giselle, from the Germanic word gisil, a pledge or noble hostage given to seal a treaty.
A respelling of Macy, an English surname from the Norman place name Massy; in the Middle Ages Macey was also a pet form of Matthew.
An English surname used as a first name, in the style of Nelson and Kelton.
The familiar short form of doctor. In the 19th-century United States, Doc and Dock were given as first names in their own right.
namesakes: Doc Holliday (Old West gambler and gunfighter)
Doc Brown (inventor in Back to the Future)

assoc.t: leader of the seven dwarfs in Disney's Snow White
Doc Martens boots, known as Docs

e.etymology: A respelling of Harley, an English place name and surname from Old English hara, hare, and leah, a woodland clearing or meadow.
A variant of Dylan, from Welsh legend, where Dylan ail Don is a sea figure of the Mabinogion; the name is usually explained as son of the sea or great tide.
e.note: This exact spelling is shared with Dylann Roof, who carried out the 2015 Charleston church shooting.

assoc.t: Dylann Roof, the 2015 Charleston church shooter

e.etymology: A modern American coinage joining the Ara- sound of Arabella and Aria with the popular -lyn ending.
A respelling of Madelyn, the English form of Madeleine, from Magdalene: Mary of Magdala, a village on the Sea of Galilee whose name means tower.
A modern American coinage joining the Tay- sound of Taylor with the -lyn ending.
A Latin American form of Justin, written the way the English name sounds to Spanish speakers. Justin comes from Latin Justinus, from justus, just.

e.meaning: summer, or rosy clouds, depending on the Chinese character
e.etymology: A Mandarin name whose meaning depends on the character: xia written one way is summer, also a common surname, and another way is the rosy glow of clouds at sunrise and sunset.
From Vietnamese Thang, the Sino-Vietnamese word for victory, to win. Thang is also a frequent element in Chin names from Myanmar.
e.note: English speakers may read it as thang, the slang spelling of thing.

e.etymology: A spelling of Zara or Zahra, from Arabic zahra, blossom or shining. The double a is common in South Asian use and is familiar from the 2004 Bollywood film Veer-Zaara.
A modern American coinage joining Ty with the -lynn ending.
From Syriac Sharbel, a name of uncertain origin borne by a 2nd-century martyr of Edessa. Lebanese families choose it for Saint Charbel Makhlouf, the Maronite monk canonized in 1977.
The Yiddish word and name Perl, pearl, matched by Hebrew Pnina and Margalit. It is still given in Yiddish-speaking Jewish communities; in the 1880s it also appeared as a spelling of Pearl.
A variant of Leilani, Hawaiian lei, a garland of flowers, plus lani, sky or heaven, reshaped with an -a ending.
